model_interpretation.claim: A one-way SIMD-prefix/scalar-suffix hybrid using bounded 64-byte ASCII blocks may amortize scan overhead versus the earlier 16-byte prefix hybrid. It skips a block only when all four SSE2 vectors are ASCII; otherwise the strict scalar decoder resumes at that block's known code-point boundary and validates the first high-bit byte rather than assuming it is a lead. Whether this granularity helps the official mixed-width n=65536 workload is unmeasured.

model_interpretation.claim: The catalog has three distinct, valid SIMD-scan programs and no repeats, but none beat the 49.62 µs baseline: the 16-byte scan measured 60.43 µs, the selected lane-bisection parent 77.82 µs, and the 64-byte variant 81.00 µs. This contrasting SIMD-prefix/scalar-remainder hybrid tests whether repeatedly restarting SIMD scans and locating a lane after each decoded code point costs more than it saves. It skips only complete 16-byte ASCII vectors; on the first vector containing any high bit, it sends the suffix from that block boundary to the strict scalar decoder. This avoids assuming the high-bit byte is a lead and preserves bounded loads, but gives up SIMD scanning of later ASCII runs. Measure it on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload; do not infer a speedup from synthetic inputs.

model_interpretation.claim: A guarded SSE2 scan that checks four adjacent 16-byte vectors as one 64-byte ASCII superblock may amortize scan-loop overhead relative to earlier 16-byte scans on long ASCII spans. If any byte in a superblock has its high bit set, the unchanged scalar scanner finds and validates it, including stray continuation bytes. The official mixed-width n=65536 workload must determine whether larger blocks help or merely add overhead.

items.subject: SIMD-assisted ASCII-run skipping with a scalar slow path
items.objective: Primary hypothesis: vector high-bit scans can skip ASCII spans while the existing strict scalar decoder handles non-ASCII code points. The benefit depends on the actual official mixed-width input containing useful ASCII spans; do not assume this or use synthetic-only results as evidence for the scored workload. Start decoding at a known code-point boundary and treat the first high-bit byte as input to validate—not as an assumed lead, since it may be a stray continuation. Keep loads and tails within n. Preserve exact validity, ABI, output, and thread budget. Measure the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and run the official ASCII/malformed correctness checks, especially for boundaries. Report this approach separately from T1's whole-buffer validation; label any hybrid distinctly and record failed variants.
